record.file_problem: No apparent file problem; the full post and comments are present.
record.tranche_reason: The post measures model loss after replacing activations with SAE reconstructions, which bears on part of V3, but it does not compare those effects with random errors of the same size.
record.gate_note: The post cites prior work on pathological SAE reconstruction errors, but those cited results are not this study’s results. Its own reconstruction-score experiments measure SAE-reconstruction interventions; they do not include a matched random-error comparison, so they cannot determine whether the errors are more harmful than random errors of the same size.
record.test_reason: This post proposes a normalized SAE architecture (NSAE) to fix feature suppression and inconsistent L0 across layers. Its own results are SAE training diagnostics: the shrinkage ratio, the L0 versus input-norm correlation, L0/L1 agreement, reconstruction score and L2 loss, all comparing NSAE with a baseline SAE. It never decomposes or characterises the SAE error. There are no linear-predictability, cross-size or random-error-matched comparisons, and no circuit or steering analysis. The reconstruction score compares two SAE architectures against zero-ablation, not against random errors of the same norm, so it cannot bear on V3. Its only contact with the claim is citing Gurnee's pathological-errors post in Related Work. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is partly right but incomplete. The author's main conclusions are that NSAE removes feature suppression, removes the correlation between layer input norm and L0, and makes L1 agree better with L0. The reconstruction-score checks show no observable performance loss and perhaps more stable training. As limitations, the author notes slightly higher L2 reconstruction loss, slower convergence, and small-scale experiments.
record.recipe_differences: The post proposes a modified SAE architecture and normalization loss; it does not reproduce the dark-matter study’s error-predictability or cross-size measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The post reports an all-layer mean reconstruction-score comparison and a separate layer-5 comparison; it also notes that matching L0 affects the comparison.

fits_no_version.finding: An architecture that removes shrinkage (feature suppression; ||x'||/||x|| near 1, Fig. 6) did not reduce reconstruction error. NSAE has slightly higher L2 reconstruction loss (Fig. 15) and a reconstruction score similar to the baseline SAE (Figs. 10, 11b). This holds on GPT-2 MLP outputs at expansion factor 16.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Removing SAE shrinkage through architectural normalization does not by itself reduce reconstruction error or downstream loss degradation. This bears loosely on whether error is a shrinkage artifact (V6), but total error is not dark matter.

record.problems: The reconstruction-score results are shown in figures without numerical values or uncertainty estimates. No random errors matched for size are tested, and the post notes that the experiments are relatively small in scale.
record.rows_left_out: No other own results were included: the remaining reported experiments concern feature suppression, L0/L1 relationships, or dictionary statistics, rather than the claim’s dark-matter error properties. Results cited from other work were excluded.

untested.parts: All of it: no regression of the SAE error on input activations.
All of it: no comparison of error norms across SAE sizes and no analysis of shared failure contexts.
All of it: no random errors of matched norm are compared with SAE reconstruction errors.
All of it: no split into linear and nonlinear error parts.
All of it: no circuit or steering analysis with or without the error term.
Not tested as stated: the post does not measure dark matter or how it changes with architecture. It only reports overall L2 and reconstruction score for one alternative architecture.

record.verdict_notes: This is a LessWrong post from April 2024, predating the original source. The reader's 'tests'/T2 classification is wrong: the reconstruction score is not a random-error comparison. Commenters note that the L0 mismatch confounds the architecture comparison. The cited Gurnee result is not this study's own result.

versions.untested_parts: Whether a large share of SAE error is linearly predictable from input activations.
Error-norm predictability across SAE sizes, shared failure contexts, and whether error persists with scale.
The study does not compare SAE reconstruction errors with random errors of the same size.
Whether the linear and nonlinear error components differ in feature content or resistance to dictionary learning.
Whether SAE-feature analyses lose model behaviour unless the error term is retained.
Whether dark matter is mostly a training artifact or shrinks with better architectures or end-to-end training.
